stages.name: Ideation
stages.question: Is there a founder with a specific problem hypothesis worth testing?
stages.primary-objective: Turn interest into a testable problem hypothesis and a committed founder.
stages.what-must-be-true: A named founder; a specific customer and problem; time available to test it.
stages.founder-challenges: Solution-first thinking; no access to customers; part-time commitment; no co-founder.
stages.expected-evidence: Written problem hypothesis; customer segment defined; founder time commitment stated.
stages.key-risks: Wasting time on an untestable idea; idea attachment.
stages.justified-interventions: Open events, hackathons, university and corporate challenges, discovery-method workshops, peer cohorts.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Testable hypothesis plus a plan for ≥20 customer conversations.
stages.next-destinations: Pre-incubation; or exit with a cheap, clear "no".

stages.name: Problem validation
stages.question: Do identifiable customers have this problem, often and painfully enough to act?
stages.primary-objective: Prove that a specific customer has the problem and cares enough to act.
stages.what-must-be-true: Systematic customer discovery is under way and the founder can name real customers.
stages.founder-challenges: Leading questions in interviews; confirmation bias; getting to buyers in B2B and government.
stages.expected-evidence: Interview log (typically 20–40 for B2C, 10–20 decision-makers for B2B); evidence of current spending or workarounds; segment ranking.
stages.key-risks: False positives from friends and family; problem is real but not a priority for the customer.
stages.justified-interventions: Discovery coaching; introductions to target customers; problem-interview reviews.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Problem confirmed in a reachable segment, with current spend or workaround documented.
stages.next-destinations: Continue pre-incubation; pivot the segment; stop.

stages.name: Solution validation
stages.question: Does the proposed solution resolve the problem in a way customers prefer to their current workaround?
stages.primary-objective: Show that the proposed solution is preferred to the current alternative.
stages.what-must-be-true: Problem validated; solution concept testable (prototype, mock-up, concierge or smoke test).
stages.founder-challenges: Over-building; pricing guesswork; technical feasibility unknown (deep tech).
stages.expected-evidence: Prototype tests; pre-commitments (LOIs, waitlists with deposits, design partners); technical feasibility for deep tech or hardware.
stages.key-risks: Polite interest mistaken for demand; the solution needs regulation or data access the startup does not have.
stages.justified-interventions: Prototype support, design-partner sourcing, light technical advice, a first regulatory check.
stages.milestone-to-progress: At least one form of commitment beyond verbal interest; a full-time founding team, or a dated plan to get there.
stages.next-destinations: DIC Incubation (entry gate); repeat; refer deep tech to a specialist partner.

stages.name: MVP / product build
stages.question: Can the team build a working product that delivers the core value?
stages.primary-objective: Build the smallest product that delivers the core value reliably.
stages.what-must-be-true: A committed team with the technical capability to build or manage the build; scope defined.
stages.founder-challenges: Technical debt; outsourced builds with no internal capability; scope creep.
stages.expected-evidence: Working MVP in users’ hands; usage data; architecture fit for the next 12 months; IP ownership clear.
stages.key-risks: The build consumes the runway before there are any customers; vendor lock-in.
stages.justified-interventions: Product and technical support, cloud credits, UX review, AI and data advisory, IP and legal basics.
stages.milestone-to-progress: MVP live with real users and instrumented usage.

stages.name: Market validation
stages.question: Will customers pay or commit (money, data, contracts) for it?
stages.primary-objective: Prove willingness to pay or commit.
stages.what-must-be-true: MVP live; a pricing hypothesis; first sales attempts.
stages.founder-challenges: Free pilots that never convert; underpricing; long B2B and government cycles.
stages.expected-evidence: Paying customers, paid pilots, signed contracts, or for deep tech, funded design-partner agreements. Revenue quality checked (no related parties).
stages.key-risks: Revenue that is really consulting; a single anchor customer; pilot purgatory.
stages.justified-interventions: First-customer access, pilot structuring with conversion clauses, pricing coaching, investor-readiness basics.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Repeated paid commitment from customers outside the founders’ network.
stages.next-destinations: DIC exit; Readiness Gate to Local Growth.

stages.name: Early traction
stages.question: Is demand recurring and coming from beyond the founders’ network?
stages.primary-objective: Show demand is recurring and can be found beyond the founders’ network.
stages.what-must-be-true: Paying customers from unaffiliated sources; usage or revenue growing month on month.
stages.founder-challenges: Founder-led sales do not scale; churn appears; cash runway is short.
stages.expected-evidence: Revenue or transaction trend, early retention cohorts, a mix of acquisition sources, first look at CAC and payback.
stages.key-risks: Growth bought with discounts; early adopters who are not the mainstream.
stages.justified-interventions: Commercial coaching, retention analysis, first institutional or angel round preparation.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Retention evidence that begins to stabilise; evidence of a viable segment.

stages.name: Product-market fit
stages.question: Do customers retain, expand and refer, with unit economics trending toward viability?
stages.primary-objective: Prove customers retain, expand and refer.
stages.what-must-be-true: Retention curves flatten; customers expand or refer; demand pulls product.
stages.founder-challenges: Premature scaling; hiring ahead of evidence; segment too broad.
stages.expected-evidence: Cohort retention (the definition varies by model, see 7.3); net revenue retention or repeat purchase; qualitative pull (Sean Ellis-type survey as a supplement, not proof).
stages.key-risks: False PMF from one segment or one large customer.
stages.justified-interventions: Acceleration: segment focus, pricing, retention engineering, unit economics.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Unit economics trending toward viable; at least one channel that is repeatable.

stages.name: Repeatable growth
stages.question: Can the company acquire customers predictably through a channel that does not depend on the founders?
stages.primary-objective: Build a growth engine that does not depend on the founders.
stages.what-must-be-true: A documented sales or acquisition playbook; a non-founder seller or channel performing.
stages.founder-challenges: Building the first sales team; finance discipline; Series A expectations.
stages.expected-evidence: Pipeline and conversion data by channel; CAC payback; a non-founder share of new revenue; audited or reviewed financials.
stages.key-risks: The channel saturates; dependence on a single large customer or government buyer.
stages.justified-interventions: Investor access (Series A), corporate and government contracts, senior hiring.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Repeatability shown over a sustained period (e.g. two or more consecutive quarters).
stages.next-destinations: Scale Gate to Scale Now; private capital; alumni.

stages.name: Scaling
stages.question: Can the organisation, capital and operations support rapid growth without breaking unit economics?
stages.primary-objective: Grow the organisation without breaking economics.
stages.what-must-be-true: Repeatable growth; a capital plan; a management layer forming.
stages.founder-challenges: Organisation design, governance, culture, capital efficiency.
stages.expected-evidence: Headcount and revenue growth with stable or improving margins; board governance.
stages.key-risks: Burn grows faster than revenue; key-person risk.
stages.justified-interventions: Mainly private: investors, boards. MCIT acts as convener and connector only.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Readiness to expand abroad, or domestic market leadership.

stages.name: International expansion
stages.question: Does the model transfer to a new market with paying customers there?
stages.primary-objective: Prove the model transfers to a new market.
stages.what-must-be-true: Qatar-anchored M7+; a target market selected on evidence.
stages.founder-challenges: Localisation, regulation, partner selection, running two markets at once.
stages.expected-evidence: Entity or partner in the target market; paying customers there; a local GTM owner; Qatar HQ retained.
stages.key-risks: Distraction from the home market; under-capitalised entry; "flag-planting" with no revenue.
stages.justified-interventions: Scale Now: market selection, missions, partner and buyer access, cost-shared.
stages.milestone-to-progress: Paying customers and a sustainable presence in at least one external market.

programs.name: DIC Pre-incubation (Explore track)
programs.program-thesis: Cheap, disciplined validation increases the share of founders who either reach a validated solution or stop early, which improves the quality of the incubation pipeline.
programs.strategic-objective: Convert M0–M1 founders into M2 teams with commitment evidence, or into an evidence-based stop.
programs.target-startup-profile: Qatar-resident individuals or teams at M0–M1 with a digital or tech-enabled problem hypothesis. Students, corporate employees and career-switchers are included. No company registration is needed.
programs.not-for: Validated teams; non-tech businesses; research projects with no customer hypothesis.
programs.entry-gates: E1: commitment (mandatory), problem specificity (35%), coachability (35%), team (30%), tech relevance and residency (mandatory).
programs.primary-interventions: Discovery sprints; buyer introductions; prototype and smoke-test kits; co-founder matching; evidence demo day.
programs.required-milestones: Interview log at the M1 standard; prototype test; commitment evidence; team decision.
programs.exit-gates: X1: M1 verified (mandatory); M2 commitment (mandatory for graduation).
programs.expected-outcomes: Validated teams for E2; early, cheap stops.
programs.next-stage-routing: Incubation gate (E2); repeat one sprint; pivot; stop; refer.
programs.kpis: Share reaching M2; share passing E2 within 6 months; cost per validated team; evidence-based stop rate (monitored).
programs.key-risks: Turning into an events program; volume targets; partner quality variance.
programs.rationale: Ideation has high failure, so cost per founder must be low; value lies in filtering and method.
programs.program-purpose: Most first-time founders fail because they build before they validate, not because the idea is bad. Pre-incubation exists to make validation cheap and fast, and to stop non-viable ideas early, before public and founder resources are committed.
programs.non-target-profile: Teams that have already validated the problem (route them to the Incubation gate); service businesses with no technology component; pure research projects with no customer hypothesis (refer to research or university programs).
programs.value-proposition: Structured discovery method, introductions to real customers, peer accountability, and a fast credible "go / pivot / stop" signal. Generic events offer exposure but not disciplined validation with feedback on evidence quality.

programs.name: DIC Incubation
programs.program-thesis: Product support combined with structured access to paying first customers turns validated solutions into products that customers pay for.
programs.strategic-objective: Move M2 teams to verified M4 (willingness to pay), with M5 emerging.
programs.target-startup-profile: Qatar-registered (or registering within the first 60 days) teams at M2–M3, with a committed founding team that can build or manage the build of a digital product. Pre-revenue is expected.
programs.not-for: Startups with recurring revenue and retention data; unvalidated ideas; long-horizon deep tech (referral track).
programs.entry-gates: E2: M1 and M2 evidence, committed team, registration within 60 days (mandatory); build capability (25%); market attractiveness (20%); cap table and IP (contextual).
programs.primary-interventions: Product and technical advisory; pilot structuring with conversion clauses; pricing coaching; first-customer introductions; investment-readiness basics.
programs.required-milestones: MVP live and instrumented (M3); first paid commitment; repeated paid commitment from unaffiliated customers (M4); metrics pack.
programs.exit-gates: X2: M3 and M4 verified; readiness basics complete (mandatory); M5 signal (directional).
programs.expected-outcomes: Startups with paying customers and a clean investment base.
programs.next-stage-routing: Readiness Gate (E3) if M5; Market Access plus hold if M4; alumni; exit.
programs.kpis: Share reaching verified M4; paid pilot conversion; time-to-M4; capital raised within 12 months; 3-year survival.
programs.key-risks: Pilot purgatory; residency drift; completion counted as graduation.
programs.rationale: The prototype-to-revenue step is where validated teams most often fail; buyer access in Qatar is a market failure MCIT can address.
programs.program-purpose: Validated teams still fail between prototype and first revenue. Their product is not robust, their pricing is untested, and they cannot get a first enterprise or government customer to commit. Incubation turns a validated solution into a product customers pay for.
programs.non-target-profile: Teams with recurring revenue and retention evidence (route to Local Growth); teams with no validated problem (Pre-incubation); deep tech needing more than 18 months of R&D before an MVP (specialist partner plus a monitored DIC relationship).
programs.value-proposition: Product support, workspace, a structured route to a first paying customer (pilot structuring, introductions to buyers), and investor-readiness basics. This combination is not available from generic coworking or online programs in a form tied to Qatar buyers.

programs.name: Local Growth Acceleration
programs.program-thesis: Focused work on retention, segment, pricing and the first non-founder channel, together with readiness-gated capital and contract access, moves early-traction startups to evidenced PMF and repeatability.
programs.strategic-objective: Move M5 startups to verified M6, with M7 emerging, and make them institutionally fundable.
programs.target-startup-profile: Qatar-anchored startups at M5 (early traction) with paying unaffiliated customers, a growing revenue or usage trend and a full-time team, typically pre-seed to seed funded or bootstrapped.
programs.not-for: Pre-revenue; already at M7; international entrants; non-scalable service businesses.
programs.entry-gates: E3 (Readiness Gate): paid unaffiliated demand, runway, Qatar anchoring (mandatory); traction trend (30%); retention signal (25%); scalability (25%); founder openness (20%).
programs.primary-interventions: Retention and cohort diagnostics; segment and pricing work; sales and channel playbook with the first non-founder seller; contract access; capital readiness and investor access.
programs.required-milestones: ICP defined; retention baseline and improvement; channel experiments; non-founder revenue; capital outcome.
programs.exit-gates: X3: M6 and unit-economics trend (mandatory); repeatable channel and capital outcome (directional).
programs.expected-outcomes: PMF-evidenced, fundable startups with an emerging growth engine.
programs.next-stage-routing: Scale Gate (E5) when M7 is verified; private capital; alumni Growth tier; 6-month reassessment.
programs.kpis: Share reaching M6; retention and NRR uplift; capital mobilised at 12 and 24 months; share reaching M7 within 18 months.
programs.key-risks: Insufficient M5 deal flow (A1); turning into a generic accelerator; hard-to-measure PMF.
programs.rationale: Closes the largest gap in the reference journey with a distinct value proposition.
programs.program-purpose: This closes the largest gap in the reference journey. Startups exit incubation with some customers but no proof of product-market fit or a repeatable channel, and they are not yet fundable by institutional investors. Nothing in the reference portfolio owns this transition.
programs.non-target-profile: Pre-revenue startups (DIC); startups already at M7 with repeatable growth (go straight to the Scale Gate or private capital); international companies new to Qatar (TASMU); lifestyle or service businesses with no scalable model.
programs.value-proposition: A hands-on commercial program focused on retention, unit economics and building the first non-founder growth channel, together with readiness-gated access to investors and to corporate and government contracts. This is the evidence that seed and Series A investors look for.

programs.name: TASMU Accelerator (Soft Landing)
programs.program-thesis: Lowering entry costs for proven international companies in priority sectors, in return for local substance, imports capability and builds Qatar-based companies.
programs.strategic-objective: Move PMF-stage international companies from Qatar market M2–M4 to paid Qatar contracts with local substance.
programs.target-startup-profile: International companies at venture maturity M6 or above in their home market, with a pilot-ready solution for a defined Qatar buyer group in a priority sector, and a stated commitment to a Qatar entity and team. In Qatar market terms they are at M2–M4.
programs.not-for: Pre-PMF companies; sales-trip seekers; firms unwilling to build substance; Qatar-anchored startups.
programs.entry-gates: E4: home-market PMF, buyer fit, substance commitment (mandatory); sector fit (20%); Qatar readiness (25%); funding capacity (25%).
programs.primary-interventions: Challenge-owner matching; regulatory and set-up navigation; localisation; local talent and partners; pilot-to-contract support.
programs.required-milestones: Entity set up; paid pilot signed; first local hire; pilot results; follow-on contract.
programs.exit-gates: X4: paid Qatar pilot or contract and substance in place (mandatory); conversion and a second customer (directional).
programs.expected-outcomes: Foreign firms operating in Qatar with contracted revenue and local staff.
programs.next-stage-routing: Market Access plus alumni Growth; Scale Now only after the substance period (A6).
programs.kpis: Paid pilot rate; pilot-to-contract conversion at 12 months; Qatar headcount and entity retention at 24 months; Qatar revenue.
programs.key-risks: Subsidising market tourism; pilot fatigue among challenge owners; nominal entities.
programs.rationale: A distinct population and value; the market axis removes overlap with Local Growth.
programs.program-purpose: Proven international companies in Qatar’s priority sectors face high entry costs: regulation, buyer access, entity set-up and local hiring. Qatar benefits when those companies bring capability and build local substance. The program lowers the entry cost in return for a real local commitment.
programs.non-target-profile: Companies seeking only a sales trip or distributor; pre-PMF companies (they would use Qatar as a test market at public cost); companies unwilling to set up local substance; Qatar-anchored startups (Local Growth).
programs.value-proposition: A structured route to Qatar buyers with pilot conversion support, regulatory navigation and set-up support. Each startup is matched to a corporate or government challenge owner. Generic investment-promotion support does not provide buyer-matched pilots.

programs.name: Scale Now
programs.program-thesis: Evidence-based market selection and pre-qualified in-market access, cost-shared and followed up, raise the success rate of Qatar-anchored companies expanding abroad.
programs.strategic-objective: Move M7+ Qatar-anchored companies to paying customers and a sustainable presence in 1–2 external markets.
programs.target-startup-profile: Qatar-anchored startups at M7 or above (repeatable growth in Qatar), with funding raised or self-funding capacity for expansion and an evidence-based shortlist of target markets.
programs.not-for: Pre-M7; nominal Qatar presence; under-capitalised firms.
programs.entry-gates: E5 (Scale Gate): M7, unit economics, verified capital, anchoring (mandatory); market evidence (30%); bandwidth (30%); regulatory transferability (40%).
programs.primary-interventions: Market selection diagnostic; pre-qualified meetings; entity and partner set-up; cross-border capital; 6–12 months of in-market follow-up.
programs.required-milestones: Market chosen; entry vehicle in place; first in-market customer; local GTM owner; repeat revenue.
programs.exit-gates: X5: entry vehicle, paying customers, Qatar HQ retained (mandatory); in-market repeatable revenue (directional).
programs.next-stage-routing: Alumni Global; exit from subsidised support; GTM service for further markets.
programs.kpis: Share with paying customers in the target market at 12 months; international revenue share; HQ retention; capital raised.
programs.key-risks: Flag-planting without revenue; HQ relocation; mission-driven rather than market-driven choices.
programs.rationale: The last subsidised step; cost-sharing and HQ conditions protect the public return.
programs.program-purpose: Qatar’s home market is small, so Qatar-anchored startups must expand to sustain growth. International entry is expensive and risky, and early mistakes such as choosing the wrong market or partner are often fatal. Scale Now lowers the cost of entering a well-chosen market while keeping the company anchored in Qatar.
programs.non-target-profile: Startups without repeatable growth at home (they would export an unproven model); companies whose Qatar presence is nominal; soft-landed international companies without at least 12 months of evidenced Qatar substance (assumption A6).
programs.value-proposition: Market selection discipline, curated buyer and partner access in target markets, trade missions with pre-qualified meetings, and support from the international network. Missions are cost-shared and tied to outcomes.

programs.name: MCIT Alumni Program
programs.program-thesis: A structured, data-linked alumni relationship captures long-term impact, recycles founder expertise into the ecosystem and catches companies that need to re-enter.
programs.strategic-objective: Maintain an active, measured alumni base that contributes back and re-enters at the right stage.
programs.target-startup-profile: Every startup that completed any MCIT program (completion, not only graduation), plus founders of companies that exited the support system.
programs.not-for: Not a channel for continued subsidy.
programs.entry-gates: Membership on completion; tier (Foundation M0–M4, Growth M5–M7, Global M8–M9) by current verified maturity; annual good standing (data return).
programs.primary-interventions: Annual check-in; maturity-matched invitations; give-back roles; fast-track reassessment.
programs.exit-gates: Lapses without good standing; responsible exit if dissolved.
programs.expected-outcomes: Survival and impact data; mentor and angel supply; re-entry pipeline.
programs.next-stage-routing: Re-entry to any program through reassessment.
programs.kpis: Data-return rate; active alumni; give-back activity; re-entry outcomes.
programs.key-risks: Low engagement; tiers seen as status rather than access.
programs.rationale: Without it, attribution and give-back capacity are lost.
programs.program-purpose: Program impact appears years after exit, and successful founders are the most credible mentors and angels. Without a structured alumni relationship, MCIT loses attribution data, give-back capacity and the ability to bring regressing companies back in.
programs.non-target-profile: Not a vehicle for continued subsidy. Alumni do not get program-level services unless they pass the relevant entry gate again.
programs.value-proposition: A peer network, deal flow visibility, invitations to investor and buyer events matched to current maturity, and a fast-track reassessment route.

gates.name: Gate E3 — Local Growth Acceleration (Readiness Gate)

criteria.name: Founder commitment
criteria.rationale: Validation needs founder time.
criteria.evidence: Time commitment statement; availability for the sprint schedule.
criteria.threshold: Enough time to run the discovery plan (indicatively ≥10 hrs/week).
criteria.exceptions: None.

criteria.name: Specific problem hypothesis
criteria.rationale: Vague ideas cannot be tested.
criteria.evidence: A written statement of who has what problem.
criteria.threshold: A named segment and a falsifiable problem.

criteria.name: Technology relevance
criteria.rationale: Mandate fit.
criteria.evidence: A description of the intended solution.
criteria.threshold: Digital or tech-enabled value.
criteria.exceptions: Non-tech ideas go to partners.

criteria.name: Coachability and learning signal
criteria.rationale: Predicts how well the founder will respond to evidence.
criteria.evidence: Response to a structured feedback exercise.
criteria.threshold: Revises at least one assumption in response to evidence.

criteria.name: Qatar residency
criteria.rationale: Mandate and program delivery.
criteria.evidence: ID or residency.
criteria.threshold: Resident in Qatar for the duration.
criteria.exceptions: Diaspora Qataris (contextual).

criteria.name: Team complementarity
criteria.rationale: Solo founders stall at M2.
criteria.evidence: Team roster.
criteria.threshold: None required at entry; this becomes a milestone.
criteria.exceptions: Solo founders admitted with a co-founder milestone.

criteria.name: Problem validated (M1)
criteria.rationale: Incubation resources should go into building, not discovering.
criteria.evidence: Interview log; evidence of current spending or workarounds.
criteria.threshold: Meets the M1 standard (Section 4).
criteria.method: Evidence review plus a sample customer call.
criteria.exceptions: None.

criteria.name: Solution commitment (M2)
criteria.rationale: Separates interest from intent.
criteria.evidence: LOIs, deposits, design-partner agreements, waitlist conversion, or a technical feasibility proof (deep tech).
criteria.threshold: At least one form of commitment beyond verbal interest from unaffiliated parties.
criteria.exceptions: Deep tech: technical proof substitutes (7.3).

criteria.name: Committed founding team
criteria.rationale: Part-time teams rarely reach M4.
criteria.evidence: Employment status; equity split; shareholder agreement.
criteria.threshold: At least one full-time founder; the others committed with dates.
criteria.exceptions: Time-bound plan accepted for university spin-outs.

criteria.name: Build capability
criteria.rationale: Outsourced-only builds create fragility.
criteria.evidence: A technical co-founder, CTO, or a managed vendor with internal product ownership.
criteria.threshold: A named product owner with the capacity to direct the build.

criteria.name: Market attractiveness
criteria.rationale: Stops incubating ventures that are too small to scale.
criteria.evidence: Bottom-up market sizing; regional relevance.
criteria.threshold: A credible path to a venture-scale or regionally scalable business.
criteria.exceptions: Strategic-sector ventures (contextual).

criteria.name: Qatar registration
criteria.rationale: Contracting, pilots and investment need a legal entity.
criteria.evidence: Commercial registration.
criteria.threshold: Registered, or registering within 60 days of entry.

criteria.name: Clean cap table and IP
criteria.rationale: Prevents later investment blockers.
criteria.evidence: Cap table; IP assignment.
criteria.threshold: Founders hold a controlling interest; IP is owned by the company or being assigned.
criteria.exceptions: University IP licensing.

criteria.name: Paid, unaffiliated demand (M4 complete)
criteria.rationale: Acceleration amplifies demand; it cannot create it.
criteria.evidence: Invoices or bank statements; contracts; customer list.
criteria.threshold: Repeated paid commitment from customers not related to the founders (indicatively 3 or more B2B, or a recurring paying base for B2C; see 7.3).
criteria.exceptions: Regulated sectors: sandbox approval plus paid design partners.

criteria.name: Traction trend (M5)
criteria.rationale: Separates a one-off sale from emerging traction.
criteria.evidence: 6-month revenue or usage series; acquisition sources.
criteria.threshold: A positive trend with at least some customers acquired outside the founder network.
criteria.exceptions: Long-cycle enterprise: pipeline quality substitutes.

criteria.name: Early retention signal
criteria.rationale: The program’s job is PMF; it needs a starting signal.
criteria.evidence: Cohort data; renewals; repeat purchases.
criteria.threshold: Retention data exists and can be analysed (no level threshold at entry).
criteria.exceptions: Fewer than 6 months of sales: admit with conditions.

criteria.name: Full-time team and runway
criteria.rationale: An acceleration program cannot fix existential cash risk.
criteria.evidence: Org chart; cash position; burn rate.
criteria.threshold: Full-time core team; runway covering the program plus 3 months, or a funding plan.
criteria.exceptions: Bridge referral to QDB or angels.

criteria.name: Qatar anchoring
criteria.rationale: Mandate.
criteria.evidence: Entity, team location, decision-makers.
criteria.threshold: Qatar-anchored (Q).
criteria.exceptions: Soft-landed companies use the Market Access service instead.

criteria.name: Growth ambition and scalability
criteria.rationale: Excludes service businesses.
criteria.evidence: Model description; gross margin.
criteria.threshold: Gross margin consistent with a scalable model for its category.
criteria.exceptions: Tech-enabled services with a credible productisation path.

criteria.name: Founder openness to change
criteria.rationale: PMF work often needs uncomfortable pivots.
criteria.evidence: Interview; DIC coach reference (if alumni).
criteria.threshold: Shows evidence-based decision-making.

criteria.name: PMF in home market (venture ≥ M6)
criteria.rationale: Qatar should not fund early market discovery for foreign companies.
criteria.evidence: Audited or reviewed financials; retention data; reference customers.
criteria.threshold: Evidence of retention and recurring revenue in at least one market.
criteria.exceptions: Deep tech with an anchor Qatar buyer (contextual).

criteria.name: Qatar buyer fit
criteria.rationale: The program’s value is matched buyers.
criteria.evidence: Named use case; challenge-owner interest.
criteria.threshold: At least one Qatar challenge owner willing to scope a paid pilot.

criteria.name: Priority-sector alignment
criteria.rationale: Strategic relevance to national priorities (DA2030 and NDS3 sectors).
criteria.evidence: Sector mapping.
criteria.threshold: Fits a declared priority sector.
criteria.exceptions: Exceptional cross-sector tech.

criteria.name: Local substance commitment
criteria.rationale: The public return is local capability.
criteria.evidence: A board-approved entry plan: entity, headcount, timeline.
criteria.threshold: A committed Qatar entity and staff plan within the program period.

criteria.name: Qatar readiness
criteria.rationale: Localisation and compliance gaps cause delays.
criteria.evidence: Data residency, Arabic and compliance assessment.
criteria.threshold: Gaps identified and closable within the program.

criteria.name: Funding capacity
criteria.rationale: Entry cost must be covered by the company.
criteria.evidence: Financial statements.
criteria.threshold: Can fund entry costs beyond program support.

criteria.name: Prior Qatar presence
criteria.rationale: Prevents subsidising firms already established in Qatar.
criteria.evidence: Registration history.
criteria.threshold: No established Qatar revenue base above the soft-landing stage.
criteria.exceptions: Re-entry after a failed earlier attempt.

criteria.name: Repeatable growth in Qatar (M7)
criteria.rationale: Exporting an unproven model multiplies risk.
criteria.evidence: Channel-level pipeline and conversion data; non-founder revenue share; 2+ quarters of data.

criteria.rationale: Expansion burns cash; economics must hold.

interventions.name: Discovery sprints (customer interview method and review)
interventions.rationale: Founders run biased interviews and read politeness as demand.
interventions.outcome: Interview log that meets the M1 evidence standard.

interventions.name: Customer and buyer introductions (through Network)
interventions.rationale: First-time founders cannot reach B2B and government decision-makers.
interventions.outcome: Decision-maker interviews in B2B segments.

interventions.name: Prototype and smoke-test toolkits
interventions.rationale: Over-building before solution testing.
interventions.outcome: Commitment evidence (LOIs, deposits, design partners).

interventions.name: Co-founder matching
interventions.rationale: Solo, part-time founders are the main reason for M2 stall.
interventions.outcome: A committed founding team at M2.

interventions.name: Evidence demo day (replaces pitch day)
interventions.rationale: Pitch days reward storytelling, not evidence.
interventions.outcome: A clear routing decision: Incubation gate, repeat, pivot or stop.

interventions.name: Product and technical advisory (architecture, UX, AI and data)
interventions.rationale: Outsourced builds without internal capability create technical debt.
interventions.outcome: An instrumented MVP live with users (M3).

interventions.name: Pilot structuring with conversion clauses
interventions.rationale: Free pilots rarely convert ("pilot purgatory").
interventions.outcome: Paid pilots or contracts (M4).

interventions.name: Pricing and commercial coaching
interventions.rationale: Underpricing and confusion about who the buyer is.
interventions.outcome: Documented pricing and buyer map.

interventions.name: First-customer introductions (corporate and government)
interventions.rationale: Access asymmetry in Qatar’s concentrated buyer market (assumption A3).
interventions.outcome: Commitments from unaffiliated customers.

interventions.name: Investor-readiness basics (cap table, data room, metrics)
interventions.rationale: Founders seek capital before they are ready, which burns investor goodwill.
interventions.outcome: A clean cap table and metrics pack, ready for the Readiness Gate.

interventions.name: Retention and cohort diagnostics
interventions.rationale: Founders confuse growth with PMF.
interventions.outcome: Verified retention evidence (M6).

interventions.name: Segment focus and pricing work
interventions.rationale: Startups sell to everyone and cannot replicate wins.
interventions.outcome: A defined ideal customer profile with improving unit economics.

interventions.name: Sales and channel playbook build, including the first non-founder seller
interventions.rationale: Founder-led sales cap growth.
interventions.outcome: A share of new revenue from non-founder channels (M7 emerging).

interventions.name: Corporate and government contract access (Market Access service)
interventions.rationale: Long, opaque procurement cycles.
interventions.outcome: Converted contracts, not pilots.

interventions.name: Capital readiness and investor access (gated)
interventions.rationale: A thin seed-to-Series-A market (assumption A2).
interventions.outcome: A priced round or term sheet, or a credible capital plan with investor feedback.

interventions.name: Challenge-owner matching with corporates and government
interventions.rationale: Foreign firms cannot identify or reach the real buyer.
interventions.outcome: Paid pilots with a named sponsor.

interventions.name: Regulatory and set-up navigation
interventions.rationale: Licensing and entity set-up delay entry.
interventions.outcome: A Qatar entity and the licences needed.

interventions.name: Localisation advisory (Arabic, data residency, procurement fit)
interventions.rationale: Products are not compliant or adapted.
interventions.outcome: A Qatar-ready product.

interventions.name: Local talent and partner access
interventions.rationale: No local delivery capacity.
interventions.outcome: Qatar-based staff and partners (substance).

interventions.name: Pilot-to-contract conversion support
interventions.rationale: Pilots stall after the program ends.
interventions.outcome: Qatar revenue under contract (Qatar market M5).

interventions.name: Market selection diagnostic
interventions.rationale: Founders choose markets by proximity or by events they have heard of.
interventions.outcome: A ranked market choice with a documented rationale.

interventions.name: Pre-qualified buyer and partner meetings (GTM Specialist)
interventions.rationale: Mission meetings rarely convert.
interventions.outcome: Qualified pipeline in the target market.

interventions.name: Entity, partner and regulatory set-up support
interventions.rationale: Entry delays and costly legal mistakes.
interventions.outcome: A legal presence or channel partner in place.

interventions.name: Growth capital access (Series A and above, cross-border)
interventions.rationale: Local capital is too thin for expansion rounds.
interventions.outcome: Expansion round or strategic investment.

interventions.name: In-market follow-up (6–12 months)
interventions.rationale: Momentum is lost after missions.
interventions.outcome: Paying customers in the target market (M9).

interventions.name: Annual maturity check-in and data return
interventions.rationale: Long-term outcomes are invisible.
interventions.outcome: A 3- and 5-year survival, revenue and jobs dataset.

interventions.name: Maturity-tiered access to services
interventions.rationale: Completion-based tiers reward history, not current need.
interventions.outcome: Services matched to where the startup is now.

interventions.name: Give-back roles (mentor, angel, speaker, buyer)
interventions.rationale: Mentor quality depends on operators.
interventions.outcome: Operator-mentors and alumni angel cheques.

interventions.name: Fast-track reassessment
interventions.rationale: Alumni who pivot or regress are lost.
interventions.outcome: Re-entry at the right stage.

services.name: Investment readiness and investor access
services.rationale: Needed from M4 to M9 in different forms. A separate program would duplicate content and expose investors to unready startups. Existing DIC investment initiatives should be folded in here (assumption A7).
services.trigger: Readiness checklist for basics (M4+); investor introductions only at M5+ with a verified metrics pack.

services.name: Investor matching and deal events
services.rationale: Investor goodwill is a shared and scarce asset.
services.trigger: Gate Panel or Portfolio Office endorsement.

services.name: Corporate innovation access and pilots
services.rationale: Used by DIC (first customers), Local Growth (contracts), TASMU (challenges). One relationship owner per corporate, as in the reference framework.
services.trigger: M4+ for pilots; a pilot standard is required (paid, success criteria, conversion path).

services.name: Government procurement
services.rationale: Procurement rules are specialised. A separate program is not justified until procurement pathways for startups are confirmed (assumption A3).
services.trigger: M4+ with a public-sector use case.

services.name: Soft landing
services.rationale: A distinct population, distinct methodology and distinct value.

services.name: International expansion
services.form: Standalone program (Scale Now) plus a light GTM service
services.rationale: Same reasoning as above. The GTM Specialist also supports ad hoc export enquiries from M7 alumni.

services.name: Founder development
services.form: Embedded in each program, plus peer circles in Alumni
services.rationale: Founder needs change with stage. Standalone leadership programs tend to drift into generic training.

services.name: Technology and product support (including AI adoption)
services.rationale: Concentrated in M2–M5 but needed across the journey. AI adoption is a capability theme, not a population, so a standalone AI program is not justified.

services.name: Legal and regulatory
services.rationale: Critical for fintech, health and data-intensive models at every stage. Regulators own the sandboxes; MCIT navigates.
services.trigger: Contextual criterion flagged at any gate.

services.name: Deep tech pathway
services.form: Referral partnership plus monitored DIC relationship
services.rationale: Timelines and capital needs do not fit cohort programs. Better served by R&D-focused partners (assumption A4).

services.name: Talent access
services.form: Cross-program light service (job board, university links)
services.rationale: Real need, but MCIT has limited levers. Revisit if hiring is shown to be the binding constraint.

services.name: Mentorship
services.form: Embedded with a shared pool tagged by stage, sector and capability (as in the reference framework)
services.rationale: Mentoring is a delivery method, not a program. Mentor matches are tied to a stated evidence gap.
services.trigger: Match requests must cite a milestone.

services.name: Alumni support
services.rationale: Required for attribution, give-back and re-entry.

routes.name: Direct entry into a later-stage program
routes.rule: Allowed when the entry gate is met. The startup gets an onboarding diagnostic to fill gaps (for example cap table, data room) through shared services.
routes.safeguard: Same evidence standard as internal progression. No "fast lane" for referrals from senior stakeholders.

routes.name: Successful progression
routes.rule: Exit-gate evidence is reused for the next entry gate, and the panel only checks what is new.
routes.safeguard: The panel includes at least one member who did not deliver the previous program.

routes.name: Graduation without immediate progression
routes.rule: Alumni status at verified maturity; reassessment every 6 months or on request; shared services available by maturity.
routes.safeguard: This counts as a positive outcome in the KPIs; it is not counted as drop-off.

routes.name: Referral to specialist support
routes.rule: Specific gap (regulatory, deep-tech R&D, financing) goes to a shared service or partner; the startup record tracks the referral and its outcome.
routes.safeguard: Referral is closed-loop: the partner confirms engagement within 30 days.

routes.name: Same maturity after completing a program
routes.rule: Recorded as completion without graduation. A diagnostic explains why (market, team, product or execution).
routes.safeguard: No re-enrolment in the same program unless there is a material change (pivot, new team member, new funding).

routes.name: Failing exit requirements
routes.rule: Options: one extension (if it is close to the gate and has a credible plan), routing to a shared service, alumni at current maturity, or a responsible exit.
routes.safeguard: Extension is capped at one. Every outcome is reported.

routes.name: Becoming ineligible
routes.rule: For example HQ relocation, misrepresented evidence, inactivity or a breach of terms: exit from the program; clawback where the agreement allows; flag in the record.
routes.safeguard: Misrepresentation leads to a defined exclusion period.

routes.name: Alumni re-entry
routes.rule: Fast-track reassessment against current maturity. A pivoted company may re-enter at an earlier stage; a grown company may enter a later program.
routes.safeguard: The re-entry decision is based on new evidence, not on loyalty.

routes.name: International startup via soft landing
routes.rule: Enters TASMU on the market axis. After graduation: Market Access service and alumni (Growth). It becomes eligible for Scale Now only after Qatar anchoring is evidenced over time (A6).
routes.safeguard: Prevents a "Qatar passport" route: a short Qatar presence followed by subsidised expansion elsewhere.

routes.name: Pivot during a program
routes.rule: Market evidence resets; the program decides whether the new direction still fits its band. If not, route to the earlier program at the next cohort.
routes.safeguard: Avoids holding pivoted startups in a program that no longer fits them.

routes.name: Startup in more than one band (strong product, weak commercial)
routes.rule: The lowest unmet mandatory criterion decides the program; strengths are used through shared services.
routes.safeguard: Prevents qualifying for several programs at once.

decisions.name: D1 — Maturity, not program completion, drives progression
decisions.recommendation: Adopt M0–M9 as the basis for every gate, KPI and routing decision.
decisions.rationale: Completion-based progression rewards attendance and creates pressure to graduate weak startups.
decisions.evidence-principle: Stage-gate principles from venture investing: capital follows evidence, not elapsed time.
decisions.implementation-implication: Startup record schema, assessor training, re-baselining of historical data.

decisions.name: D2 — Two-axis assessment
decisions.recommendation: Assess venture maturity and market position separately.
decisions.rationale: International and local startups at the same company maturity need different interventions.
decisions.evidence-principle: Market-entry risk is market-specific; firms proven at home still have to validate in each new market.
decisions.implementation-implication: TASMU and Scale Now gates are defined on the market axis.

decisions.name: D3 — Local Growth owns the PMF band
decisions.recommendation: Re-scope Local Growth to M5→M7 with PMF as a mandatory exit.
decisions.rationale: This is the widest gap and the costliest failure point, and no current program owns it.
decisions.evidence-principle: PMF is the main predictor of follow-on fundability; premature scaling is a common failure mode.
decisions.implementation-implication: Program design for the AOP submission; vendor specification focused on commercial and retention work.

decisions.name: D4 — Independent gates
decisions.recommendation: A Gate Panel with external members decides the Readiness and Scale gates.
decisions.rationale: Removes the incentive conflict for programs judging their own outputs.
decisions.evidence-principle: Separating delivery from assurance is a basic control principle.
decisions.implementation-implication: Recruit 6–10 rotating external panellists; panel terms of reference.

decisions.name: D5 — Services, not new programs
decisions.recommendation: Capital, market access, regulation and technology run as cross-program services.
decisions.rationale: Needs span several stages; separate programs would add handovers and duplicate cohorts.
decisions.implementation-implication: Service catalogue update; maturity triggers in the catalogue.

decisions.name: D6 — Light, open pre-incubation
decisions.recommendation: Remove registration; keep costs low; deliver mostly through partners.
decisions.rationale: Ideation has high volume and high failure, so the cost per founder must stay low.
decisions.evidence-principle: At early stages the value is in cheap filtering, not in deep support.
decisions.implementation-implication: Partner model with universities and community; evidence demo days.

decisions.name: D7 — Qatar substance conditions
decisions.recommendation: Substance tests for TASMU graduation and soft-landed access to Scale Now.
decisions.rationale: Protects the public return on support given to foreign firms.
decisions.evidence-principle: Conditional incentives are standard in investment attraction.
decisions.implementation-implication: Payroll and registry verification; legal review of clawback terms.

decisions.name: D8 — Maturity-based alumni tiers
decisions.recommendation: Alumni tier reflects current verified maturity; membership reflects completion.
decisions.rationale: Access to scarce services should follow need and readiness, not history.
decisions.implementation-implication: Annual alumni check-in becomes mandatory for access.

risks.name: Gate inflation under pressure to report numbers
risks.mitigation: Independent panel; publish definitions; pair graduation with 12-month outcomes.

risks.name: Portfolio Office capacity
risks.mitigation: Phase in assessment depth; analyst support from the vendor contract; tooling.

risks.name: Insufficient M5+ deal flow for Local Growth
risks.mitigation: Rolling admission or small cohorts; direct-entry marketing; validate with baseline data first (A1).

risks.name: Corporate and government pilot fatigue
risks.mitigation: Pilot standard (paid, scoped, conversion path); one owner per partner.

risks.name: Disruption to active cohorts
risks.mitigation: Apply new gates to new intakes only; TASMU Cohort 4 (Jul–Dec 2026) unchanged, as in the reference roadmap.

risks.name: Founder perception of "harder" programs
risks.mitigation: Communicate gates as a fast way to get the right support; publish routing feedback.

assumptions.name: No other national program serves M5–M7 Qatar-anchored digital startups at scale.
assumptions.ifWrong: Make Local Growth a co-delivery or referral partnership.

assumptions.name: The local angel and seed market is thin for M4–M6 startups.
assumptions.ifWrong: If the market is deep, reduce Capital Readiness to matchmaking and shift resources to Market Access.

assumptions.name: Access to corporate and government buyers is the main commercial constraint in Qatar, and procurement can accommodate startups.

blocks.text: The reference framework (MCIT Enablement Programs Integrations Framework, September 2026) gets the operating model broadly right: one section, one startup record, shared capabilities, common gates and an alumni loop. Its weakness is the program architecture underneath. Stages are defined by programs rather than by startup maturity, the gates test attributes that are easy to present and hard to verify, and the most consequential development step in a startup’s life — moving from early traction to product-market fit — has no clear owner.

This architecture rebuilds the portfolio from the startup outward. It starts with what must become true about a venture at each step, defines the evidence that proves it, and only then assigns programs. The result keeps all five reference propositions, but sharpens each one and changes how startups move between them.
Seven headline recommendations

Adopt a 10-stage Venture Maturity Model (M0–M9) as the single language for entry, exit, routing and reporting. Programs map to maturity bands; completing a program never moves a startup up a stage on its own.

Assess maturity on two axes: venture maturity and market position. An international company can be at repeatable growth at home but at market validation in Qatar. The reference framework conflates the two, which is why TASMU Soft Landing and Scale Now sit awkwardly in the same funnel.

Give Local Growth Acceleration one job: take startups from early traction to evidenced product-market fit and a first repeatable acquisition channel (M5 → M7). This closes the biggest gap in the current journey and removes its overlap with DIC.

Reposition DIC Pre-incubation as a light, high-volume, open-access track with no company-registration requirement. Requiring registration at ideation adds cost before the idea is tested, and conflicts with the reference entry gate that already asks for a validated problem.

Separate "completion", "graduation" and "qualification". Completion = finished the program. Graduation = met the program exit gate. Qualification = met the entry gate of a different program, assessed independently.

Make gate decisions independent of the program that delivered the support. Program leads present evidence; a Gate Panel with at least one external investor or operator decides Readiness and Scale gates. This removes the incentive to over-graduate.

Run investment readiness, market access/pilots, regulatory navigation and specialist technical support as cross-program services, not new programs. Each is needed at several stages, and turning them into programs would create more handovers and duplicate cohorts.

WHERE INSTITUTIONAL SUPPORT SHOULD STOP
Direct MCIT support should taper once a startup has (a) evidenced repeatable growth, (b) raised priced institutional capital or is self-funding growth, and (c) entered at least one market outside Qatar with paying customers. blocks.text: 2.1 What the portfolio is for

Thesis: MCIT should increase the number of Qatar-anchored technology companies that reach repeatable growth and expand internationally. It does this by lowering the cost and time of generating credible evidence at each maturity step, while correcting specific market failures that private capital and markets will not correct on their own.

That makes the portfolio an evidence-generation system, not a training system. Every intervention exists to help a startup produce the next piece of decision-grade evidence (problem, solution, willingness to pay, retention, unit economics, repeatability, transferability to a new market) faster and more cheaply than it could alone.

blocks.text: 2.3 Where support begins and where it stops
Begins at M0, but at very low cost per founder. The aim at ideation is to grow the pool of capable founders and to filter cheaply, not to incubate ideas.

Intensity peaks at M5–M7. This is where the gap between "has customers" and "has a business" is widest, where failure is most expensive, and where public support has the clearest value (access to corporate and government buyers).
Stops at sustained M9, or earlier when private capital and customers already meet the startup’s needs. Continuing subsidies beyond this point crowds out private providers and ties up scarce capacity.
2.4 How the programs work as one portfolio
One maturity language. All programs use M0–M9, so a startup’s position is described the same way everywhere.
One front door, one assessment. A startup is placed by evidence, so direct entry at any stage is normal, not an exception.
Non-overlapping maturity bands. Each program owns a band. Where two programs touch a band (Local Growth and TASMU around M5–M7), they differ on the market axis, not the venture axis.
Shared services follow the startup. Capital readiness, market access, regulatory navigation and technical support are drawn on by any program when the startup’s maturity justifies it.
Independent gates. Moving between programs needs a separate qualification decision, so no program can push startups into the next one.
2.5 Underlying logic chain

rows: Defined by what has been proven, not by time spent or programs completed.
Each stage has a primary evidence question. Evidence must be verifiable by a third party.
The gap between current evidence and the evidence the next stage needs.
Justified only if it closes that gap faster, cheaper or more credibly than the startup could alone, and the gap reflects a market failure.
A new piece of verified evidence that moves the startup up a stage, or an early, cheap "no" that frees founder time and public money.

PRINCIPLE
A fast, evidence-based "stop" or "pivot" is a valid portfolio outcome. A portfolio that only measures progression will push founders to fake progress.

blocks.text: The reference journey has six stages (Discover, Ideate, Incubate, Accelerate, Scale, Alumni). Four of these are named after programs and one (Alumni) is a relationship status, so the model describes where the startup is in MCIT, not how mature the startup is. The model below replaces it as the diagnostic layer. The reference stages remain as a simple communication layer for external use.
3.1 Axis 1 — Venture maturity (M0–M9)

rows: Is there a founder with a specific problem hypothesis worth testing?
Do identifiable customers have this problem, often and painfully enough to act?
Does the proposed solution resolve the problem in a way customers prefer to their current workaround?
Can the team build a working product that delivers the core value?
Will customers pay or commit (money, data, contracts) for it?
Is demand recurring and coming from beyond the founders’ network?
Do customers retain, expand and refer, with unit economics trending toward viability?
Can the company acquire customers predictably through a channel that does not depend on the founders?
Can the organisation, capital and operations support rapid growth without breaking unit economics?
Does the model transfer to a new market with paying customers there?

blocks.text: Solution validation (M2) and MVP (M3) often happen together for software. They stay separate because deep tech and hardware startups may spend 12–36 months in M3 with no customer revenue, and the model must not class them as failing.
3.2 Axis 2 — Market position

rows: Qatar entity, Qatar-based decision-makers and core team; Qatar is the home or primary market.
Company proven elsewhere; Qatar maturity measured separately, usually M2–M4 in the Qatar market.
Qatar-anchored company entering one or more external markets; maturity is tracked per target market.

WHY TWO AXES MATTER
Without the market axis, an international company with US$m revenue and a Qatar-founded startup with ten customers both look like "acceleration stage". They need very different things. With two axes, TASMU Soft Landing is defined as "venture ≥ M6, Qatar market M2–M4" and Scale Now as "venture ≥ M7 in Qatar, target market M0–M2". The overlap disappears.

blocks.text: 3.3 Maturity is evidence, not time
A startup is assessed at the highest stage for which all mandatory evidence is verified. Partial evidence for a higher stage is recorded as "emerging", but it does not change the stage.
Maturity can go down: a pivot to a new customer segment usually resets market evidence to M1–M2, while team and technical evidence carry over.
Maturity is reassessed at every gate and once a year for alumni. The startup record keeps the full history, so time-in-stage can be analysed.

Each stage is defined below. The "appropriate interventions" column shows what is justified at that stage, which may come from a program, a shared service, or an outside partner. Stage-to-program mapping is in Section 5.

blocks.text: 7.1 Gate design principles

Three layers. (1) Mandatory knock-outs that test eligibility and safety. (2) A weighted maturity score that tests evidence against the stage definition. (3) Contextual adjustments for business model, sector and regulation.
Evidence over assertion. Each criterion names the artefact that proves it and how it is verified (document, data access, customer reference call, technical review).
